displayTitle: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals

scope.note: OpenAI claims undecidability of rational solvability for arbitrary integer-coefficient polynomials, with the number of variables part of the input. This is the rational variant of Hilbert's tenth problem. The manuscript does not claim an existential definition of the integers in the rationals.

originalQuestion: Hilbert's 1900 tenth problem requested a finite procedure deciding whether a polynomial equation with integer coefficients has an integer solution. His phrase 'rational integers' means ordinary integers, not arbitrary rational numbers.
modernQuestion: Is there an algorithm which, given n and f in Z[X₁,…,Xₙ], decides whether f has a zero in Qⁿ? Equivalently, is the existential theory of rational arithmetic decidable? Allowing fractions changes the domain of the unknowns, even when coefficients remain integers.
questionDifference: Hilbert's integer problem was negatively resolved in 1970. The October 2026 manuscript claims a negative answer to the rational variant in all numbers of variables. Robinson's 1949 undecidability theorem concerns the full first-order theory, allowing universal as well as existential quantifiers; it does not already settle this question. Diophantine definitions or models of integer arithmetic in Q would be sufficient ways to transfer undecidability, but the 2026 paper instead claims a Turing reduction using a computable sequence of rational-solvability tests. It does not establish either such definition or model. Its arithmetic inputs include a companion pointwise 2-converse for elliptic curves with rational two-torsion, under a 2-primary Selmer corank condition of zero or one; that input is not a claim of the full Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture.

conceptualOrigins.label: 1900: inherited algorithmic question about Diophantine equations

firstFormulation.label: Rational variant: explicitly discussed by 2000; first proposer unlocated

attribution: Hilbert names the ancestor, not a located original proposer of the rational variant. Robinson's 1949 paper is an early conceptual precursor. The earliest explicit rational existential-decision discussion located in this batch is Cornelissen–Zahidi's 2000 introduction; Poonen's 2003 paper states the polynomial version directly. Neither is claimed as the historical first formulation. Classification: inherited problem with gradual crystallization through logic and arithmetic geometry.

contributors.name: David Hilbert
contributors.contribution: Posed the integer-solvability decision problem in 1900.

contributors.name: Julia Robinson

uncertainty: The first proposer and first printed formulation of the rational variant remain unlocated. The 2000 source supplies an explicit discussion, not a priority claim. Choosing 1900 as the conceptual starting point foregrounds the algorithmic question; a longer history of Diophantine equations would begin much earlier. Mazur's conjecture is used here as a conditional obstruction, not an established theorem or a prediction of decidability. OpenAI's claims and dependency statements have been read but their proofs have not been independently assessed.

events.title: An algorithm requested before algorithms had a formal theory
events.description: Hilbert asks for a finite procedure deciding integer solvability of arbitrary polynomial equations. The wording presupposes an effective method, rather than anticipating that impossibility itself could be proved.
events.relationNote: Conceptual ancestor of the rational question; not the same domain.

events.title: Rational arithmetic is already undecidable—with more quantifiers
events.description: Robinson defines the integers inside the rationals and proves their full first-order arithmetic undecidable. Universal and existential quantifiers both appear: knowing this still leaves the equation-solvability question unanswered.
events.relationNote: A nearby result makes quantifier complexity central to the inherited problem.

events.title: From exponential equations to ordinary polynomials
events.description: Davis, Putnam and Robinson represent recursively enumerable relations using exponential Diophantine equations in 1961. Matiyasevich's Fibonacci construction in 1970 removes exponentiation, completing the negative solution over integers.
events.relationNote: Settles the ancestor; transfer to rational unknowns requires another argument.

events.title: Geometry threatens the standard transfer route
events.description: Mazur's topology conjecture predicts finitely many connected components in closures of rational points and would exclude an existential definition of Z in Q. Cornelissen–Zahidi extend this conditional obstruction to Diophantine models in 2000.
events.relationNote: An obstructed construction need not make the decision problem decidable.
events.uncertainty: The original 1992 article was located bibliographically; the 1995 updated formulation was read.

events.title: Undecidability reaches rings almost as large as Q
events.description: Poonen constructs proper subrings Z[S⁻¹] with undecidable Diophantine theory even when S has natural density one among primes. The method uses selected multiples of a point on a rank-one elliptic curve.
events.relationNote: A constructive branch develops alongside the geometric obstruction; density one does not give the whole rational field.

events.title: The complement of the integers becomes existentially definable
events.description: Koenigsmann gives a universal definition of Z in Q, equivalently a Diophantine definition of Q minus Z. This sharply reduces quantifier complexity without providing the existential definition of Z that would immediately transfer the integer theorem.
events.relationNote: Closer definability results are not interchangeable with rational solvability.

events.title: The release claims the rational decision problem is undecidable
events.description: OpenAI claims no algorithm can decide rational zeros of integer-coefficient polynomials, for arbitrary input n. Its proposed reduction uses a sequence of rational-solvability tests and arithmetic control from companion results, rather than asserting a Diophantine model of Z in Q.
events.relationNote: These predecessors explain the problem and available methods; timeline links do not certify the new proof.
events.uncertainty: This is a reported theorem, without independent proof review. The source snapshot includes a 7 October companion manuscript.

questionPlainLanguage: Could a single algorithm decide whether any polynomial equation has a solution made of fractions? It must always finish and correctly answer yes or no, however many unknowns the equation contains.
questionFormal: Given $n\geq 1$ and $f\in\mathbb{Z}[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$, is there an algorithm that always terminates and decides whether there exists $x\in\mathbb{Q}^n$ with $f(x)=0$? The number of variables is part of the input. Undecidability means that no such algorithm exists; it does not mean that every individual equation is unanswerable.
whyItMatters: Finding a solution and certifying that none exists are very different tasks. We can systematically enumerate rational tuples and test them: if a solution exists, this search eventually finds one. If none exists, it runs forever. The question asks whether another procedure can always recognize both outcomes. Over integers, polynomial equations can encode arbitrary computation, which explains why a universal decision procedure is impossible. Fractions add solutions and remove the integer domain that this encoding relies on; clearing denominators introduces a requirement to find integer solutions and does not supply a rational decision algorithm. Understanding whether computation can still be encoded links mathematical logic to the arithmetic geometry of rational points on curves and higher-dimensional varieties.
illustrativeExample: For $2x-1=0$, there is **no integer solution**, but there is the **rational solution $x=\frac12$**. This illustrates the change of domain; it is not evidence for undecidability. The challenge is one procedure for every polynomial, rather than solving this easy example.
historicalHook: Hilbert’s name survives on a question he did not formulate in its modern form: his 1900 problem asked about integers, not fractions.
whatAIClaims: OpenAI reports a proof that no algorithm can decide rational solvability for every integer-coefficient polynomial, with no fixed limit on the number of variables. If correct, this would give a negative answer to the modern rational decision problem. The manuscript claims a reduction using sequences of rational-solvability tests, rather than an existential definition of the integers inside the rationals.
whatRemainsOpen: The manuscript does not claim an existential definition or Diophantine model of the integers in the rationals; those stronger encoding questions remain outside its result. Its companion elliptic-curve input is not the full Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture. This site has not independently assessed the proof, so the rational decision problem is presented here as a claimed resolution pending independent assessment.
questionSummary: Can an algorithm always decide whether a polynomial equation has a rational solution?
claimSummary: rational undecidability; full resolution of the decision problem
